sentences.text: Siats is known from a single partial postcranial skeleton, specimen FMNH PR 2716, which is housed at the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago.
The Siats holotype — the specimen the species is based on — represents a single individual that was skeletally immature at the time of death, indicated by unfused neural arches.
Siats is defined by seven unique anatomical traits, four of which are autapomorphies specific to the genus.
Distinctive features of Siats include subtriangular distal tail vertebrae, elongated laminae on proximal tail vertebrae, a concaved acetabular rim, and a notch on the lateral brevis shelf.
Siats possessed broad neural spines on its dorsal vertebrae.
Siats is considered one of the largest known theropod dinosaurs from the mid-Cretaceous period in North America.
Researchers estimated Siats to be approximately 10 meters long and weigh about 3.9 metric tons based on femur circumference regression.
Despite being skeletally immature, the Siats holotype was estimated to be as large as the adult Allosaurus anax and Acrocanthosaurus.
The dinosaur Siats was first described by paleontologists Lindsay E. Zanno and Peter J. Makovicky in 2013.
The genus name Siats refers to a man-eating monster from Ute mythology.
The species name meekerorum honors geologist John Caldwell Meeker and his family for supporting paleontological research.
The holotype specimen of Siats was discovered by Lindsay Zanno during a 2008 Field Museum expedition led with Peter Makovicky.
The genus Siats contains only one known species, Siats meekerorum.
Siats was initially classified as a megaraptoran, a group of large theropods with debated evolutionary relationships.
Scientists have proposed alternative classifications for Siats within the groups Neovenatoridae, Allosauroidea, and Tyrannosauroidea.
A 2025 analysis by Kellermann, Cuesta, and Rauhut consistently placed Siats within Megaraptora based on shared pneumatic fossa positions.
Siats fossils were collected from the Mussentuchit Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation in Utah, dating to the early Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous about 94.5 million years ago.
The fossil record for Siats spans the Cenomanian stage, from approximately 100.5 to 93.9 million years ago.
A 2014 study contested Siats' placement in Megaraptora, suggesting megaraptorans were likely tyrannosauroids rather than neovenatorids like Siats.

Bell et al. (2016) found Siats' phylogenetic position uncertain, with analyses placing it variously as a relative of ornithomimosaurs, a basal megaraptoran, or a tyrannosauroid closer to tyrannosaurids than Xiongguanlong.
Naish and Cau (2022) recovered Siats as the most basal megaraptoran and suggested it and Chilantaisaurus represented a wave of gigantism in tyrannosauroids before the Tyrannosauridae evolved.
